lessons.title: Sound recognition: consonant clusters and contracted forms
lessons.objective: Pronounce consonant clusters, distinguish sounds and use contracted forms in rapid speech.
lessons.course:
Consonant clusters are two or three consonants together: str (street, strong), spr (spray), pl (plate), cl (clinic), tr (treat), sk (skin). We pronounce every consonant without adding a vowel: “street”, not “sitreet”.
Contracted forms join two words with an apostrophe: I am → I’m, do not → don’t, it is → it’s, we will → we’ll, he has not → he hasn’t.
lessons.model: The adult says slowly, then fast: “The strong nurse sprays the clinic.” “I’m fine, but I don’t feel strong.”
lessons.guided: Say ten words with clusters, slowly then quickly. Turn five sentences into contracted forms.
lessons.exercise: What is the contracted form of “do not”?
lessons.remediation: Tap the consonants on the table as you say them.
lessons.transfer: Use three contracted forms when you talk at home.

practice.prompt: Match the full form and the contracted form.
Which word begins with a three-consonant cluster?
Listen and repeat quickly.
practice.listen: The strong nurse sprays the clinic. I’m fine, but I don’t feel strong.

lessons.title: Reading silently: a visit to the district hospital
lessons.objective: Read a text silently and answer questions about it.
lessons.course: Before reading, look at the title and guess what the text is about. Read the questions, then read silently. Find the sentence that answers each question.

support.title: Read silently
support.text: On Monday, Bih had a high fever. Her mother took her to the district hospital. They waited in the queue until a nurse called them. The nurse took Bih’s temperature: 39 °C. The doctor examined her and asked for a blood test. It was malaria. Bih received tablets and was told to sleep under a treated net. Three days later, she was back at school.

lessons.model: The adult reads the title, guesses aloud, then reads the questions and finds the first answer.
lessons.guided: Read the questions, then the text silently. Answer in full sentences.
lessons.remediation: Find the answers by underlining key words in the text.
lessons.transfer: Tell your family what to do when someone has a fever.

practice.prompt: What was Bih’s temperature?
Put the events in order.
items: The doctor asked for a blood test.

practice.prompt: After how many days was Bih back at school?

lessons.title: Dictation: the apostrophe s’ for many owners
lessons.objective: Use s’ for plural owners and write dictated sentences and a paragraph correctly.
lessons.course:
When the owners are plural and end in s, we add only an apostrophe: the nurses’ room (the room of the nurses), the doctors’ meeting, the patients’ beds. Irregular plurals take ’s: the children’s ward, the women’s clinic.
In a dictation: listen to the whole sentence first, write, then reread to check spelling and punctuation.
lessons.model: The adult dictates: “The nurses’ room is next to the children’s ward.” and shows the two apostrophes.
lessons.guided: Write a dictation of four sentences about a health centre. Check each apostrophe.
lessons.exercise: Rewrite: the room of the nurses.
lessons.remediation: First decide: one owner (’s) or many owners (s’)?
lessons.transfer: Write three phrases about your family with s’ or ’s.

practice.prompt: One owner or many? Choose.
Complete.
practice.text: the doctors[[’|']] cars; the children[[’s|'s]] toys

practice.prompt: Listen and write the dictation.
practice.listen: The nurses’ room is clean. The children’s ward is on the left. Visitors wash their hands at the door.

lessons.title: Pronouns: subject, object, possessive and relative
lessons.objective: Identify and use subject, object, possessive and relative pronouns in sentences.
lessons.course:
Subject pronouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Object pronouns: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. Possessive pronouns: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.
Relative pronouns join two ideas: who (people), which (things), that (people or things), whose (owner). “The nurse who helped me is kind.” “The tablets which I took were bitter.”
lessons.model: The adult says: “This is the doctor. He treated me.” → “This is the doctor who treated me.”
lessons.guided: Replace nouns with pronouns in five sentences. Join four pairs of sentences with who or which.
lessons.exercise: Join: I saw the nurse. She vaccinated the baby.
lessons.answer: I saw the nurse who vaccinated the baby.
accept: I saw the nurse who vaccinated the baby
I saw the nurse that vaccinated the baby
lessons.remediation: Use who for people and which for things.
lessons.transfer: Describe three people you know using “who”.

practice.prompt: Match each subject pronoun with its object pronoun.
practice.explanation: Object pronouns come after the verb.

practice.prompt: Complete with who or which.
practice.text: The boy [[who]] fell is better. The medicine [[which]] he took is strong.
practice.explanation: who for people; which for things.

practice.prompt: This bag is my bag. It is …

lessons.title: Proper, improper and mixed fractions: sharing medicine and food
lessons.objective: Identify proper and improper fractions and mixed numbers and convert between them.
lessons.course:
Proper fraction: the numerator is smaller than the denominator: ¾, 2/5. Improper fraction: the numerator is bigger or equal: 7/4, 5/5.
Mixed number: a whole number and a fraction: 1¾. 7/4 = 1¾ because 4/4 = 1 whole and ¾ is left. 2½ = 5/2.
lessons.model: The adult cuts 2 loaves into quarters and gives 7 quarters: 7/4 = 1 whole loaf and ¾.
lessons.guided: Use paper circles to show 5/3, 9/4 and 3/2. Write each as a mixed number.
lessons.remediation: Shade the shapes, count the wholes, then the parts left.
lessons.transfer: Describe a meal shared in your family with fractions.

practice.prompt: Which fraction is improper?
3½ = ?/2. Write the numerator.
Match each fraction with its kind.

lessons.title: Mass: grams and kilograms at the health centre
lessons.objective: Establish the relationship between g and kg and convert and compare masses.
lessons.course:
1 kg = 1 000 g. Half a kilogram = 500 g; a quarter = 250 g.
At the health centre, babies are weighed in kg: 4 kg 300 g = 4 300 g. To compare masses, write them in the same unit.
lessons.model: The adult reads a baby scale: “The baby weighs 5 kg 200 g, that is 5 200 g.”
lessons.guided: Read the mass on five food packets. Convert each into g or kg and g. Order them from lightest to heaviest.
lessons.exercise: How many grams are there in 3 kg?
lessons.remediation: Use a scale and 1 kg packets to compare.
lessons.transfer: Read the mass on packets in your kitchen.

practice.prompt: A baby weighed 3 kg 500 g at birth and 5 kg 100 g at two months. How many grams did the baby gain?
Which is heavier?
How many 250 g packets make 1 kg?

lessons.title: Area of rectangles and squares: the floor of a clinic room
lessons.objective: Calculate the area of rectangles and squares in square units.
lessons.course:
The area is the space covered by a shape. We count squares or use a formula. Rectangle: A = length × width. Square: A = side × side.
A room 5 m long and 4 m wide has an area of 20 m² (square metres).
lessons.model: The adult draws a rectangle on squared paper, counts the squares, then multiplies length × width.
lessons.guided: Draw five rectangles on squared paper and find their area by counting, then with the formula.
lessons.exercise: A rectangle is 7 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its area?
lessons.remediation: Count the squares row by row.
lessons.transfer: Estimate the area of your bedroom floor in square metres.

practice.prompt: A square tile has sides of 6 cm. Area in cm²?
Which unit measures area?
A room has an area of 24 m² and a width of 4 m. What is its length, in m?

lessons.title: Ranking data: heights and masses of pupils
lessons.objective: Arrange data in ascending and descending order and find the greatest and the smallest.
lessons.course:
Ascending order goes from the smallest to the greatest; descending order goes from the greatest to the smallest.
Heights in cm: 128, 135, 122, 140 → ascending: 122, 128, 135, 140. The range is greatest − smallest = 18 cm.
lessons.model: The adult measures four children and writes their heights, then ranks them.
lessons.guided: Measure the heights of five family members. Rank them in ascending and descending order. Find the difference between the tallest and the shortest.
lessons.remediation: Find the smallest first, cross it out, then find the next.
lessons.transfer: Rank your family members by age.

practice.prompt: Put the masses in descending order.
practice.explanation: From the greatest to the smallest.
